raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old woman presented with erythematous papules, papulopustules, and a plaque on the right lower limb of more than two years duration without other symptoms. Before her presentation here, she had visited multiple other hospitals. After the diagnoses of dermatitis and eczema, she was treated orally with antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine, and ebastine, and topical glucocorticoid ointments, such as mometasone furoate and halometasone. However, the lesions did not respond to treatment, and the rash gradually increased. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus for more than 10 years and a tattoo on her right lower limb acquired two years before the lesion onset. After her diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, she was taking metformin orally (0.5g three times a day). In the first half of the year, the glycemia control was satisfactory, generally at 6-7 mmol/L (fasting) and 9-10 mmol/L (postprandial). However, the patient failed to regularly monitor her glycemia levels for a long period because she had not experienced any symptoms. As the patient remembered, her postprandial glycemia were generally 20-30 mmol/L around tattooing and 13-15 mmol/L around lesion onset (see Figure 1). She denied any use of immunosuppressive agents, or immunodeficient disorders. 
The physical examination revealed only the presence of a cutaneous lesion on the right lower limb and red and blue-black tattoos (Figure 2A). The human immunodeficiency virus test was negative. Results of the laboratory tests for routine blood, T and B lymphocyte subpopulations, renal and hepatic functions, Treponema pallidum hemagglutination, rapid plasma reaction, and immune indices were the normal range. Specifically, the immune index test measures levels of anti-nuclear antigen and anti-extractable nuclear antibodies, immunoglobulins, and complement. 
A KOH (potassium hydroxide) examination revealed visible fungal hyphae under the microscope (Figure 3A). A lesion biopsy specimen was cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 C, and numerous and identical fungal colonies grew that were dense, and grey-black in appearance (Figure 3B). Microscopically, the colonies were characterized by septate and hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia 2.5 to 3 microm in diameter, produced in chains basipetally from single palisade-like layer phialides that were borne directly on broadly clavate vesicles (Figure 3C). The pathogen was identified as A. fumigatus based on these characteristics and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation-time of flight mass spectrometry. 
The histopathological examination of the skin biopsy revealed a reticulate corneous layer, oval spores in the corneous layer, a slightly thickened epidermis, and in the superficial dermis a few infiltrating lymphocytes and neutrophils around the blood vessels in the superficial dermis (Figure 4A). Periodic acid-Schiff staining was positive, and spores were observed in the cuticle (Figure 4B). Therefore, the patient was given a diagnosis of PCA based on the clinical manifestation, histopathology, and culture, and the exclusion of infection in other systems. 
Treatment included oral itraconazole (200 mg/d) and local wound care with ciclopirox olamine 1% ointment. One month after initiating treatment there had been gradual improvement to a certain extent in most lesions (Figure 2B). Complete resolution of lesions was achieved three months after initiating treatment (Figure 2C). There was no report of any adverse event during the treatment period. Until now, no recurrence has been observed after 6 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a >2-year history of refractory erythematous papules, papulopustules, and a plaque over a tattoo site on her right lower extremity.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over 2 years prior to presentation (2 years after acquiring a red and blue-black tattoo on her right leg during a period of severe postprandial hyperglycemia of 20-30 mmol/L), the patient developed erythematous papules, papulopustules, and an enlarging plaque over the right lower limb. Multiple outside hospital courses of oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, ebastine) and potent topical corticosteroids (mometasone furoate, halometasone) failed to halt progression.
subjective.past_medical_history: 10-year history of poorly monitored type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral metformin 0.5 g three times daily (postprandial blood glucose 20-30 mmol/L at the time of right leg tattooing 4 years ago, and 13-15 mmol/L at lesion onset 2 years ago). No history of immunosuppressive drug use or primary immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic non-healing papulopustular plaque on the right leg; negative for systemic symptoms. Home medication: metformin 0.5 g TID; prior ineffective topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed erythematous papules, papulopustules, and a scaly plaque overlying a red and blue-black tattoo on the right lower extremity, with an otherwise normal systemic physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, liver and renal function tests, T- and B-lymphocyte subset counts, ANA, ENA, immunoglobulins, complement, HIV test, and syphilis serologies (TPHA and RPR) were all normal or negative. Direct KOH microscopy of skin scrapings demonstrated septate fungal hyphae.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy histopathology (H&E and PAS stain) revealed hyperkeratosis with numerous PAS-positive oval fungal spores within the stratum corneum and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic and neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Fungal culture of the biopsy tissue on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 C grew dense grey-black colonies with septate hyaline hyphae and clavate vesicles bearing uniseriate phialides and basipetal chains of 2.5-3 um columnar conidia, confirmed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry as Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed primary cutaneous aspergillosis (PCA) caused by Aspergillus fumigatus arising in a lower-extremity tattoo in a patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (nodular secondary/tertiary syphilis and HIV excluded via negative TPHA, RPR, and HIV tests). Treated with oral itraconazole 200 mg daily and topical ciclopirox olamine 1% ointment, achieving partial regression at 1 month, complete clinical clearance at 3 months, and zero recurrence over 6 months of follow-up.
